title: U.S. Wholesale Inflation Hits 6.5%—What It Means for Bitcoin’s Next Move
summary: U.S. wholesale inflation reached its highest annual rate since November 2022, but the monthly pace slowed sharply. Bitcoin faces a more complicated signal than the headline suggests.
content:
Skip to content
Assets: BTC

U.S. wholesale inflation reached its highest annual rate since November 2022, but the monthly pace slowed sharply. Bitcoin faces a more complicated signal than the headline suggests.

Bitcoin’s inflation problem has a fresh complication. U.S. wholesale prices rose 6.5% over the year to October, their fastest annual increase since November 2022, even as the monthly pace cooled sharply.

The November 13 Producer Price Index release offers ammunition for two competing readings: the latest month was less severe, but the accumulated inflation problem remains substantial. For cryptocurrency investors, the key question is which message carries more weight with the Federal Reserve.

Bitcoin inflation outlook: a slower month, a hotter year

Final-demand producer prices increased 0.3% in October, compared with a revised 1.4% in September. The annual rate nevertheless climbed from 6.3% to 6.5%. These measures answer different questions: the first tracks one month, while the second compares prices with a year earlier.

The measure excluding food, energy and trade services rose 0.5% for the month and 4.9% annually. That detail complicates any argument that a softer headline monthly figure settles the inflation debate.

Energy prices at the final-demand level edged lower, while goods and services prices increased. The release therefore does not present a simple picture of falling energy costs eliminating pressure throughout the economy.

The BLS defines PPI as a measure of selling prices received by domestic producers. It is distinct from the prices households pay and from the personal consumption expenditures measure targeted by the Fed. Comparing its 6.5% reading directly with the Fed’s 2% goal would mix different indexes.

The Fed had already warned that a pause was not a pivot

At its October 28 meeting, the Federal Open Market Committee held its policy rate at 3.75%–4%. Two members, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, preferred a quarter-point increase. The committee’s statement said: “Inflation remains elevated.”

That split matters. Holding rates steady can provide time to assess incoming information without signalling that the next move will be a cut. Investors who treat every pause as easing risk misreading the decision.

Governor Christopher Waller made the distinction explicit in his November 10 speech, saying “further tightening of monetary policy will be needed, sooner rather than later.” He supported at least a quarter-point December increase under his expected outlook and said a stronger move might be warranted if inflation proved worse.

Waller spoke before that day’s consumer inflation release and before Friday’s PPI figures. His remarks establish the concerns policymakers brought into this week; they are not a reaction to the new wholesale-price report or a commitment by the full committee.

He also singled out the AI infrastructure buildout as a potential source of price pressure, alongside energy costs. That connects two markets often treated as separate stories: enthusiasm for more computing capacity can support investment while raising concerns about the cost of equipment and power.

For crypto readers, the implication is a feedback loop to watch, rather than a demonstrated cause of Bitcoin’s decline. Strong technology investment is not automatically a signal that financing conditions will become easier for every risky asset.

Why Bitcoin can struggle when inflation rises

Bitcoin’s fixed supply underpins its long-term scarcity argument. Its market price, however, is set by buyers and sellers facing changing financing costs and competing investment choices. Those are separate mechanisms.

If persistent inflation keeps interest rates higher, cash and interest-bearing assets can become more competitive, while borrowing to take market exposure becomes more expensive. That can work against speculative demand even when the underlying inflation story sounds favourable to scarce assets.

It does not follow that every inflation release must push Bitcoin lower. Expectations matter: a troubling number can be less troubling than investors had anticipated. Positioning, liquidity and subsequent policy commentary can also change the response.

That is why this report should not be assigned sole responsibility for a move already under way. BNC’s latest Bitcoin market analysis describes November 13 trading around $68,600–$69,200 alongside negative funding on several exchanges. Those observations document a weak market; they do not isolate the effect of PPI.

Three signals that would clarify the next move

First, watch whether subsequent Fed communication treats the slower monthly increase as progress or focuses on persistent underlying pressure. The next scheduled policy meeting is December 8–9, leaving room for more data and debate.

Second, distinguish price stabilisation from renewed buying. A market can stop falling because leveraged positions have been closed, without attracting enough fresh demand to sustain an advance. ETF flows and spot-market activity would help test that distinction, using figures dated to the same trading session.

Third, assess funding rates alongside price. Negative funding indicates demand for short exposure relative to long exposure in perpetual futures. It can accompany weakness, but it can also leave a market vulnerable to a squeeze if prices recover. It is context, not a forecast.

The strongest reading of Friday’s release is therefore conditional. A slower monthly pace offers evidence that the pressure can ease; the annual rate and underlying measure show why policymakers may remain unconvinced. Bitcoin’s next durable move needs more than a comforting interpretation of one headline.

title: Weekly Review: eToro Crypto Trades Fall 62%; IG Group Secures Court Approval for Jersey Move
summary:
The futures prop trading sector faced renewed
questions over its business model, with exchange data costs and low-priced
challenges putting pressure on firms operating without recurring subscriptions.
Meanwhile, established industry figures returned with new businesses, while
brokers continued to ex...
content:
The futures prop trading sector faced renewed questions over its business model, with exchange data costs and low-priced challenges putting pressure on firms operating without recurring subscriptions. Meanwhile, established industry figures returned with new businesses, while brokers continued to expand their regulatory and corporate structures.

London's trading industry is coming home!

The week also brought developments in brokerage technology, corporate governance and retail trading activity. IG Group advanced its planned move to Jersey, CFI secured preliminary approval for a crypto brokerage operation in Dubai, and eToro reported weaker crypto trading activity despite account growth.

Artificial intelligence, prediction markets and technology disruptions also featured among the week’s developments.

Futures Prop Firms Face Rising CME Data Costs Under One-Time Pricing Models

Several futures proprietary trading firms have moved away from monthly subscriptions towards one-time challenge fees, raising questions about the sustainability of their pricing models. Apex, Tradeify, Bulenox and My Funded Futures made the shift in 2026, while exchange data costs continue to recur monthly for active users.

CME’s real-time annual licence fee is $29,280 per exchange, although many firms access data through platform vendors rather than licensing it directly. TradersYard’s co-founder Manuel Sonnleithner said a prop-specific simulation licence requires all four exchanges, bringing the base fee to $117,120 annually, before additional monthly data charges.

The mismatch between recurring operating costs and one-off customer payments remains a central challenge.

Futures Prop Firms See Margins Squeezed by $49 Challenges and Rising Costs

The pressure on futures prop firms extends beyond exchange data fees, with lower challenge prices and higher operating costs reducing profitability. TradersYard CEO Manuel Sonnleithner, citing internal industry data, estimated that net margins have fallen from 25-30% to 10-15%. Platform expenses, including monthly charges per user, make low-priced challenges harder to sustain.

Ruben Abitbol of RUBIK said futures firms generally face higher operating costs than CFD prop firms, partly because of platform and market-data expenses. Payout ratios also differ, with futures firms typically paying out 70-80% compared with 40-50% for CFD firms, according to Abitbol’s broad benchmark.

Several operators, including FundingTicks, Rev One and FundedSeat, closed during 2026, and Alpha closed its Premium Plan.

Former iS Prime Founders Launch New Liquidity Business for Brokers

Three former iS Prime executives have launched JT Prime, a prime-of-prime liquidity provider targeting brokers, funds, family offices and proprietary trading firms.

Raj Sitlani and Jonathan Brewer, who co-founded iS Prime in 2014, established the business alongside Jeff Wilkins, who previously led iS Prime’s risk analytics operation.

JT Prime will offer aggregated Tier 1 bank and non-bank liquidity across foreign exchange, precious metals and index CFDs, with FIX API connectivity.

The business operates as the institutional arm of retail broker JT Markets. JT Markets currently holds a Seychelles licence, while an application in an unnamed Western market remains pending. The founders also plan to expand into digital assets.

CFI Receives Preliminary VARA Approval for Dubai Crypto Brokerage

CFI Financial Group has received in-principle approval from Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority, known as VARA, for its crypto brokerage subsidiary, CFIX. The approval covers broker-dealer services, but the company cannot begin offering virtual asset services until it receives a full licence.

According to CFI, VARA requires the subsidiary to finalise its leadership appointments, operational infrastructure, governance arrangements and regulatory controls before granting final authorisation. CFI said CFIX would operate as a separate legal entity with its own governance structure.

The development adds another regulatory step to the group’s international expansion. CFI also holds authorisations in several jurisdictions, including Brazil, where it received approval for a securities brokerage earlier this year.

IG Group Advances Jersey Redomiciliation Ahead of November Listing Switch

IG Group secured court approval for its proposed move from England and Wales to Jersey, bringing the restructuring closer to completion. The transition will establish a new Jersey-incorporated holding company, Jenkins Topco, which will be renamed IG Group Holdings.

The move is scheduled to take effect on 13 November, subject to delivery of the court order to the Registrar of Companies. Existing shares will be cancelled, with new shares issued through the Jersey entity.

The current shares are scheduled to be delisted from the London Stock Exchange on 16 November, when the new shares are expected to begin trading. The group expects restructuring costs of £30 million in 2026.

CFI Chairman Says Independent Board Must Challenge Management Decisions

CFI Financial Group’s independent chairman, Federico Cirulli, outlined how the board oversees management as the broker expands its operations and regulatory footprint. Cirulli said independent directors should pressure-test management proposals rather than routinely block decisions.

The board sets strategic direction, establishes risk appetite and holds executives accountable, while Chief Executive Ziad Melhem manages daily operations. Cirulli also said founder-led structures are effective in the early stages, but that more stakeholders, a more complex offering and heavier regulation can call for a different structure.

CFI reported $3.45 trillion in trading volume during the third quarter, up 123% year-on-year, while nine-month volume reached $8.8 trillion, figures that are company-reported. Cirulli said governance and internal controls must keep pace with that expansion.

eToro Reports 62% Drop in Crypto Trades Despite Funded Account Growth

eToro’s clients placed 2 million cryptocurrency trades in October, down 62% from a year earlier, despite an 18% increase in funded accounts to 4.42 million. The average amount invested per crypto trade fell 29% to $228.

The figures followed a weaker third quarter, when net income dropped 74% year-on-year to $15 million and net contribution declined 13% to $186 million. Adjusted EBITDA fell 56% to $34.2 million.

Net trading income from equities, commodities and currencies increased 21% to $88.5 million, although it declined from the previous quarter. Chief Financial Officer Meron Shani said crypto activity had recovered sequentially compared with the second quarter.

eToro Targets $100 Million Latin American Revenue After Argentine Acquisition

eToro plans to generate $100 million in Latin American revenue within two to three years, using its proposed acquisition of Argentine fintech LB Finanzas as a regional base. The company agreed to acquire the investing and payments app for less than $20 million.

Chief Executive Yoni Assia gave analysts the target, and the article noted that eToro already has a larger online audience in the region than most retail brokers, according to FM Intelligence data.

The acquisition marks the company’s fourth deal announced in 2026, following purchases involving Zengo and Bit2C and an agreement to acquire US broker TradeZero. Assia said eToro would slow its acquisition activity to focus on integrating the businesses.

AI Trading Agents Create New Monitoring Challenges for Forex Brokers

Artificial intelligence agents are increasingly able to interact directly with retail trading accounts, creating new monitoring challenges for forex and CFD brokers, according to an op-ed by Marios Kyriakou, Head of FX Dealer Academy by Your Bourse.

Connections through platforms such as MetaTrader and cTrader allow AI tools to access trading functions through Model Context Protocol, or MCP, servers. These integrations can make it difficult for dealing desks to distinguish automated orders from trades placed manually by clients.

Remote setups may also involve access tokens held by third-party AI tools, limiting brokers’ visibility. While some official integrations offer read-only access and approval requirements before trades are executed, open-source and custom-built alternatives may lack similar safeguards. The development raises questions about client profiling, exposure management and operational risk.

AI Voice Agents Raise Questions About Client Trust in Forex Brokerage

Forex brokers are increasingly considering AI voice agents to handle customer acquisition and routine communications. The technology can contact prospective clients, chase account-opening documents through a secure upload link, follow up on incomplete applications and schedule calls with human representatives.

However, its use in client-facing conversations raises concerns about mis-selling and the boundaries of automated communication. Anish Lal, Chief Business Development Officer at BlackBull Markets, argued that voice agents should support administrative tasks rather than provide trading advice or encourage additional deposits, and that documents and card details should never be taken over the phone.

He also highlighted the importance of transparency, including informing customers when they are speaking to AI. Brokers must balance efficiency gains with appropriate controls and maintain human involvement where financial decisions and client trust are concerned.

Prediction Markets Seek Broker Partnerships to Sustain Trading Activity

Prediction market operators are increasingly turning to brokerage partnerships and wider product offerings to attract customers beyond major sporting and political events, according to a column by Paul Golden. The World Cup generated a significant increase in activity, but platforms now face the challenge of maintaining user engagement between major events.

Women are less than 25% of the user base on prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket… but are the largest consumers on Instagram and Facebook. I think Meta’s prediction market product will actually be a huge hit due to this untapped audience and the social/cultural topics they are interested in. Count me in for predicting who gets voted out next on Love Island. 🏝️

— Brit Morin 🦞 (@brit) July 7, 2026

Kalshi has expanded its distribution through partnerships with Alpaca and Public, allowing event contracts to reach customers through existing brokerage platforms. It has also introduced products beyond conventional event contracts, including a stock index perpetual future.

The expansion brings prediction markets closer to traditional financial products. However, regulatory uncertainty, particularly around sports-related contracts in the US, remains a challenge for operators seeking broader distribution.

Nvidia Shares Fall More Than 6% Following Jensen Huang’s Resignation

Nvidia shares fell more than 6% in trading after the announcement that co-founder Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and board member after 33 years leading the company, although the sell-off had begun before the announcement.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO while retaining her CFO responsibilities, and the board is considering internal and external candidates for a permanent successor. Former Synopsys chief executive Harvey Jones was appointed as Nvidia’s first board chairman.

The company did not state a reason for the departure, which followed an independent investigation announced by the board, which appointed former acting US Attorney Joon Kim and law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct the review. Jones said operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap would continue without interruption.

Microsoft 365 Outage Disrupts Financial Markets and Broker Operations

A global Microsoft 365 outage disrupted financial firms across several markets, forcing trading desks and brokerages to rely on manual workarounds. The disruption, which had lasted 12 hours at the time of reporting, affected Exchange Online, with Downdetector recording more than 130,000 reports in the US at its peak.

Brokerages in Singapore and India reported delays in customer support, while CMC Markets in Singapore used phone calls and WhatsApp to bypass affected systems. Japanese financial firms also turned to manual processes as email authentication failures disrupted trade confirmations and settlements, and a Kalshi post joked that Japanese markets had switched to fax machines.

The outage highlighted the industry’s dependence on cloud-based services, with retail FX brokers also reporting difficulties involving customer logins and operational processes.

The futures prop trading sector faced renewed questions over its business model, with exchange data costs and low-priced challenges putting pressure on firms operating without recurring subscriptions. Meanwhile, established industry figures returned with new businesses, while brokers continued to expand their regulatory and corporate structures.

London's trading industry is coming home!

The week also brought developments in brokerage technology, corporate governance and retail trading activity. IG Group advanced its planned move to Jersey, CFI secured preliminary approval for a crypto brokerage operation in Dubai, and eToro reported weaker crypto trading activity despite account growth.

Artificial intelligence, prediction markets and technology disruptions also featured among the week’s developments.

Futures Prop Firms Face Rising CME Data Costs Under One-Time Pricing Models

Several futures proprietary trading firms have moved away from monthly subscriptions towards one-time challenge fees, raising questions about the sustainability of their pricing models. Apex, Tradeify, Bulenox and My Funded Futures made the shift in 2026, while exchange data costs continue to recur monthly for active users.

CME’s real-time annual licence fee is $29,280 per exchange, although many firms access data through platform vendors rather than licensing it directly. TradersYard’s co-founder Manuel Sonnleithner said a prop-specific simulation licence requires all four exchanges, bringing the base fee to $117,120 annually, before additional monthly data charges.

The mismatch between recurring operating costs and one-off customer payments remains a central challenge.

Futures Prop Firms See Margins Squeezed by $49 Challenges and Rising Costs

The pressure on futures prop firms extends beyond exchange data fees, with lower challenge prices and higher operating costs reducing profitability. TradersYard CEO Manuel Sonnleithner, citing internal industry data, estimated that net margins have fallen from 25-30% to 10-15%. Platform expenses, including monthly charges per user, make low-priced challenges harder to sustain.

Ruben Abitbol of RUBIK said futures firms generally face higher operating costs than CFD prop firms, partly because of platform and market-data expenses. Payout ratios also differ, with futures firms typically paying out 70-80% compared with 40-50% for CFD firms, according to Abitbol’s broad benchmark.

Several operators, including FundingTicks, Rev One and FundedSeat, closed during 2026, and Alpha closed its Premium Plan.

Former iS Prime Founders Launch New Liquidity Business for Brokers

Three former iS Prime executives have launched JT Prime, a prime-of-prime liquidity provider targeting brokers, funds, family offices and proprietary trading firms.

Raj Sitlani and Jonathan Brewer, who co-founded iS Prime in 2014, established the business alongside Jeff Wilkins, who previously led iS Prime’s risk analytics operation.

JT Prime will offer aggregated Tier 1 bank and non-bank liquidity across foreign exchange, precious metals and index CFDs, with FIX API connectivity.

The business operates as the institutional arm of retail broker JT Markets. JT Markets currently holds a Seychelles licence, while an application in an unnamed Western market remains pending. The founders also plan to expand into digital assets.

CFI Receives Preliminary VARA Approval for Dubai Crypto Brokerage

CFI Financial Group has received in-principle approval from Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority, known as VARA, for its crypto brokerage subsidiary, CFIX. The approval covers broker-dealer services, but the company cannot begin offering virtual asset services until it receives a full licence.

According to CFI, VARA requires the subsidiary to finalise its leadership appointments, operational infrastructure, governance arrangements and regulatory controls before granting final authorisation. CFI said CFIX would operate as a separate legal entity with its own governance structure.

The development adds another regulatory step to the group’s international expansion. CFI also holds authorisations in several jurisdictions, including Brazil, where it received approval for a securities brokerage earlier this year.

IG Group Advances Jersey Redomiciliation Ahead of November Listing Switch

IG Group secured court approval for its proposed move from England and Wales to Jersey, bringing the restructuring closer to completion. The transition will establish a new Jersey-incorporated holding company, Jenkins Topco, which will be renamed IG Group Holdings.

The move is scheduled to take effect on 13 November, subject to delivery of the court order to the Registrar of Companies. Existing shares will be cancelled, with new shares issued through the Jersey entity.

The current shares are scheduled to be delisted from the London Stock Exchange on 16 November, when the new shares are expected to begin trading. The group expects restructuring costs of £30 million in 2026.

CFI Chairman Says Independent Board Must Challenge Management Decisions

CFI Financial Group’s independent chairman, Federico Cirulli, outlined how the board oversees management as the broker expands its operations and regulatory footprint. Cirulli said independent directors should pressure-test management proposals rather than routinely block decisions.

The board sets strategic direction, establishes risk appetite and holds executives accountable, while Chief Executive Ziad Melhem manages daily operations. Cirulli also said founder-led structures are effective in the early stages, but that more stakeholders, a more complex offering and heavier regulation can call for a different structure.

CFI reported $3.45 trillion in trading volume during the third quarter, up 123% year-on-year, while nine-month volume reached $8.8 trillion, figures that are company-reported. Cirulli said governance and internal controls must keep pace with that expansion.

eToro Reports 62% Drop in Crypto Trades Despite Funded Account Growth

eToro’s clients placed 2 million cryptocurrency trades in October, down 62% from a year earlier, despite an 18% increase in funded accounts to 4.42 million. The average amount invested per crypto trade fell 29% to $228.

The figures followed a weaker third quarter, when net income dropped 74% year-on-year to $15 million and net contribution declined 13% to $186 million. Adjusted EBITDA fell 56% to $34.2 million.

Net trading income from equities, commodities and currencies increased 21% to $88.5 million, although it declined from the previous quarter. Chief Financial Officer Meron Shani said crypto activity had recovered sequentially compared with the second quarter.

eToro Targets $100 Million Latin American Revenue After Argentine Acquisition

eToro plans to generate $100 million in Latin American revenue within two to three years, using its proposed acquisition of Argentine fintech LB Finanzas as a regional base. The company agreed to acquire the investing and payments app for less than $20 million.

Chief Executive Yoni Assia gave analysts the target, and the article noted that eToro already has a larger online audience in the region than most retail brokers, according to FM Intelligence data.

The acquisition marks the company’s fourth deal announced in 2026, following purchases involving Zengo and Bit2C and an agreement to acquire US broker TradeZero. Assia said eToro would slow its acquisition activity to focus on integrating the businesses.

AI Trading Agents Create New Monitoring Challenges for Forex Brokers

Artificial intelligence agents are increasingly able to interact directly with retail trading accounts, creating new monitoring challenges for forex and CFD brokers, according to an op-ed by Marios Kyriakou, Head of FX Dealer Academy by Your Bourse.

Connections through platforms such as MetaTrader and cTrader allow AI tools to access trading functions through Model Context Protocol, or MCP, servers. These integrations can make it difficult for dealing desks to distinguish automated orders from trades placed manually by clients.

Remote setups may also involve access tokens held by third-party AI tools, limiting brokers’ visibility. While some official integrations offer read-only access and approval requirements before trades are executed, open-source and custom-built alternatives may lack similar safeguards. The development raises questions about client profiling, exposure management and operational risk.

AI Voice Agents Raise Questions About Client Trust in Forex Brokerage

Forex brokers are increasingly considering AI voice agents to handle customer acquisition and routine communications. The technology can contact prospective clients, chase account-opening documents through a secure upload link, follow up on incomplete applications and schedule calls with human representatives.

However, its use in client-facing conversations raises concerns about mis-selling and the boundaries of automated communication. Anish Lal, Chief Business Development Officer at BlackBull Markets, argued that voice agents should support administrative tasks rather than provide trading advice or encourage additional deposits, and that documents and card details should never be taken over the phone.

He also highlighted the importance of transparency, including informing customers when they are speaking to AI. Brokers must balance efficiency gains with appropriate controls and maintain human involvement where financial decisions and client trust are concerned.

Prediction Markets Seek Broker Partnerships to Sustain Trading Activity

Prediction market operators are increasingly turning to brokerage partnerships and wider product offerings to attract customers beyond major sporting and political events, according to a column by Paul Golden. The World Cup generated a significant increase in activity, but platforms now face the challenge of maintaining user engagement between major events.

Women are less than 25% of the user base on prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket… but are the largest consumers on Instagram and Facebook. I think Meta’s prediction market product will actually be a huge hit due to this untapped audience and the social/cultural topics they are interested in. Count me in for predicting who gets voted out next on Love Island. 🏝️

— Brit Morin 🦞 (@brit) July 7, 2026

Kalshi has expanded its distribution through partnerships with Alpaca and Public, allowing event contracts to reach customers through existing brokerage platforms. It has also introduced products beyond conventional event contracts, including a stock index perpetual future.

The expansion brings prediction markets closer to traditional financial products. However, regulatory uncertainty, particularly around sports-related contracts in the US, remains a challenge for operators seeking broader distribution.

Nvidia Shares Fall More Than 6% Following Jensen Huang’s Resignation

Nvidia shares fell more than 6% in trading after the announcement that co-founder Jensen Huang had resigned as president, chief executive and board member after 33 years leading the company, although the sell-off had begun before the announcement.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress has taken over as interim CEO while retaining her CFO responsibilities, and the board is considering internal and external candidates for a permanent successor. Former Synopsys chief executive Harvey Jones was appointed as Nvidia’s first board chairman.

The company did not state a reason for the departure, which followed an independent investigation announced by the board, which appointed former acting US Attorney Joon Kim and law firm Wachtell, Lipton, Rosen & Katz to conduct the review. Jones said operations, customer commitments and the product roadmap would continue without interruption.

title: Bitcoin ETFs shed $2.35B in 2 weeks, BlackRock’s losing streak hits 11
summary: US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $185.4 million in net outflows Friday, with BlackRock’s IBIT accounting for $143.5 million and Fidelity’s FBTC shedding $41.9 million.
content:
MarketsPublishedNov 14, 2026

US spot Bitcoin ETFs recorded $185.4 million in net outflows Friday, with BlackRock’s IBIT accounting for $143.5 million and Fidelity’s FBTC shedding $41.9 million.

US spot Bitcoin exchange-traded funds (ETFs) recorded $2.35 billion in net outflows over two consecutive weeks, as redemptions reached more than $1 billion each week. 

According to Farside Investors data, spot Bitcoin ETFs shed $1.07 billion between from Monday to Friday, following $1.28 billion in outflows the previous week, the largest weekly redemptions since late June. 

The funds recorded $185.4 million in net outflows on Friday, down from $284.1 million on Thursday and $299.8 million on Wednesday. BlackRock’s iShares Bitcoin Trust (IBIT) accounted for $143.5 million of Friday’s withdrawals, while Fidelity’s Wise Origin Bitcoin Fund (FBTC) shed $41.9 million. 

Friday marked the seventh consecutive trading session of net withdrawals, with about $1.71 billion redeemed since Nov. 5. The sustained outflows coincided with broader market weakness as Bitcoin (BTC) fell below $70,000 on the same day. 

BlackRock’s Bitcoin ETF extends losing streak to 11 sessions

IBIT’s $143.5 million in net outflows on Friday extended the fund’s withdrawal streak to 11 consecutive trading sessions since Oct. 30. 

The latest losses brought IBIT’s total net outflows during the streak to about $2.35 billion.

IBIT’s November outflows reached $2.12 billion, accounting for roughly 90% of the spot Bitcoin ETF market’s net withdrawals.

  • Examine where brokers can find sustainable growth as acquisition costs rise and established markets become more competitive.

Established acquisition markets are crowded, client acquisition costs are rising and brokerage product offerings often look remarkably alike. For firms planning growth in 2027, the more useful question is which new markets, products and partnerships have actually delivered results.

xecutives from across the industry gathered at the Finance Magnates Summit London 2026 aim to examine growth strategies they have tested, from product diversification to regional expansion and partnerships.

Growth in retail brokerage is becoming harder to secure through familiar acquisition channels alone. Competition in established markets, rising acquisition costs and increasingly similar product propositions mean that commercial teams must be more selective about where they invest. The session will focus on strategies that firms have tested rather than forecasts that sound attractive on paper.

Speakers will consider where new products and assets have generated demand, how automation influences the client journey and which regional or partner channels remain commercially viable. They will also examine the costs behind expansion: setting up entities, meeting operational requirements and supporting customers after the first conversion.

The session is relevant to leaders responsible for acquisition, product, partnerships and profitability. A promising market is only valuable if a business can enter it sustainably, and a new feature matters only if it improves client outcomes or commercial performance. The aim is to help delegates frame sharper questions about their own growth plans for 2027.

title: U.S. Targets $1.2 Billion From Binance Hack—Where Is the Rest?
summary: U.S. authorities have court authority over more than $1.2 billion from the Binance hack. Binance says it has replaced affected assets, while the hunt for stolen coins continues.
content:
Skip to content
Assets: BNB ETH

U.S. authorities have court authority over more than $1.2 billion from the Binance hack. Binance says it has replaced affected assets, while the hunt for stolen coins continues.

The Binance hack recovery has reached a significant milestone: U.S. authorities say more than $1.2 billion in stolen cryptocurrency is subject to court-authorized seizure or restraint. But that headline leaves a much larger question unanswered: what happens to the rest?

The Justice Department’s November 12 announcement puts the broader frozen total above $2.7 billion following the October theft. Crucially, the $1.2 billion is included in that figure. Adding the two would exaggerate the recovery, while calling either sum customer repayments would go further than the announcement supports.

Separately, Binance says it has completed coverage of the affected assets, having committed more than $6.34 billion in company funds to source replacement tokens through market and over-the-counter purchases. Its update says withdrawals continue reopening in phases.

That is a distinct milestone: replacing assets from company resources restores backing without recovering the original coins from the attackers. The law-enforcement totals should therefore not be read as a measure of how much Binance has replaced for customers.

Binance hack recovery: three numbers, three meanings

The FBI attributes the attack to North Korea’s TraderTraitor actors and dates the theft to around October 29. Its alert values the stolen assets at more than $6 billion.

That is the starting point. The frozen total describes assets intercepted by government and private-sector efforts. The court-authorized figure identifies a portion covered by seizure or restraint authority. Those are stages of intervention, rather than three separate piles of money.

“We worked together to freeze this massive criminal fraud in its tracks,” U.S. Attorney Jeanine Ferris Pirro said in the DOJ statement.

The language matters because a successful interception is not the end of a recovery. Establishing control, resolving legal claims and determining how assets can be returned are different questions. The announcement gives no timetable for completing that process.

The trail runs through Ether and crypto’s trading infrastructure

The FBI’s October 31 alert said investigators had observed stolen assets being converted primarily into Ether. It warned of further laundering through decentralised finance and instant-swap services and published addresses associated with the operation.

Its appeal extended beyond large exchanges to THORNode operators, RPC providers, DeFi services and blockchain analytics firms. That breadth illustrates the problem: stopping a theft’s proceeds requires action across the routes used to move and exchange them.

Public ledgers can preserve a transaction trail without guaranteeing that every destination can freeze assets. Investigators need both visibility and a point where someone can act. A traceable transfer and a recoverable balance are not the same thing.

For readers following the numbers, a precise remaining-loss estimate would be premature. These are dollar valuations of crypto assets, and the authorities describe lower bounds. Without matching valuation times and complete balances, subtracting one headline from another produces an impression of precision the disclosures do not provide.

A separate operation exposes the human weakness

The same enforcement announcement addressed FaceStealer, a separate North Korean social-engineering campaign. The FBI’s dedicated account of the scheme describes attackers hijacking communication accounts, recording victims’ webcams and using convincing imposter video meetings to compromise new targets.

According to the bureau, that campaign caused more than $400 million in theft over 18 months. Investigators seized over 900 victims’ webcam recordings. Those figures belong to FaceStealer and should not be added to the Binance recovery figures as though they describe one incident.

The disturbing element is the use of familiarity. A message can arrive through a compromised account belonging to someone the target knows. Recorded footage can then make an imposter meeting look like a conversation with a trusted contact.

The FBI also warns that open-source developers and maintainers are being targeted. Access to a developer’s software repository can put downstream users at risk, extending the consequences beyond whatever cryptocurrency is on the initial victim’s device.

Why a blockchain audit is only part of the defence

The implication is uncomfortable for technically sophisticated users: recognising a face, a familiar username or a plausible work request is insufficient authentication. Verification needs a separate route that the suspicious conversation does not control.

A request to install software or change a device during an unexpected meeting deserves particular scrutiny. For teams, the useful question is whether one compromised employee account can reach both operational systems and valuable assets. Separating those permissions can limit the damage.

This is a different threat from a flaw in Bitcoin’s underlying software. BNC’s Bitcoin Core security disclosure coverage explains why identifying the affected layer matters. A sound protocol does not protect a user who grants an attacker access to a device or signing process.

What would make the next update meaningful?

The most useful follow-up would distinguish newly frozen assets from previously announced balances, identify progress toward final recovery and explain whether funds have actually been returned. A larger number alone may conceal very different legal and operational outcomes.

The Binance case shows both sides of crypto’s transparency: stolen funds can remain visible as they move, yet visibility does not automatically stop them. The recovery effort has established a substantial foothold. The unanswered story is how much of that foothold can become a completed recovery—and how much remains beyond reach.

For exchanges, the practical test is readiness before the next incident: knowing who can authorise a response, preserving records and maintaining contact with the services that might receive stolen assets. A recovery operation becomes harder when those relationships must be assembled after funds have started moving.

title: OpenAI launches AI payments in ChatGPT with Visa, Mastercard and Amex
summary: OpenAI’s new payment wallet lets AI agents complete purchases using existing card networks, with plans to eventually allow preauthorized transactions.
content:
Latest NewsPublishedNov 13, 2026

OpenAI’s new payment wallet lets AI agents complete purchases using existing card networks, with plans to eventually allow preauthorized transactions.

OpenAI on Friday introduced a new feature allowing AI agents to make purchases on behalf of users directly within ChatGPT through existing payment networks, in collaboration with American Express, Mastercard and Visa.

The wallet lets users authorize transactions using biometric verification, such as facial recognition or fingerprints. Payment networks generate tokenized card credentials for each approved purchase, keeping users’ actual card details from merchants and AI agents, the company said.

The service is being rolled out to ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US with eligible cards issued in the country. OpenAI said it plans to eventually support purchases within preset spending limits and other restrictions without requiring approval for each transaction.

The launch comes as AI companies seek to move beyond product recommendations into executing transactions, potentially changing how consumers interact with online merchants. OpenAI said it is working with payment processors and fraud prevention firms to support AI purchases through existing checkout systems.

OpenAI joins a growing field of companies developing payment systems for AI agents. Google introduced its Agent Payments Protocol in 2025, while Visa and Mastercard have launched initiatives to support AI-initiated transactions.

Crypto companies are also developing payment infrastructure for AI agents. Coinbase introduced its x402 protocol in 2025, enabling autonomous stablecoin payments for digital services, while Circle launched its Agent Stack in May, allowing agents to hold and spend USDC within predefined limits. Crossmint, which provides stablecoin infrastructure, has taken a different approach, combining stablecoin wallets with traditional card networks.

Global agentic commerce transaction value is expected to reach $1.5 trillion by 2030, according to an April report from Juniper Research, up from an estimated $8 billion in 2026.

title: Adam Back makes case for simpler security as Blockstream launches Bitcoin custody system
summary: Blockstream’s new custody system, developed with Thales, uses dedicated hardware for transaction signing as Adam Back advocates for offline security to reduce cyber risks.
content:
Adam Back’s Bitcoin infrastructure company Blockstream has launched a new institutional digital asset custody solution developed with French technology group Thales, as the cryptographer pushes for simpler, offline security systems to protect Bitcoin against increasingly sophisticated cyberattacks.

The solution, announced Friday, combines Thales’ hardware security modules (HSMs) with Blockstream’s Secure Multi-Party Computation (Secure-MPC) technology, allowing institutions to authorize transactions while keeping sensitive cryptographic operations within dedicated security hardware, according to the company.

Unlike conventional MPC implementations that may perform portions of the signing process outside dedicated security hardware, Blockstream said its architecture executes the entire signing protocol within the protected environment of Thales’ HSMs.

Blockstream co-founder and CEO Adam Back, a pioneering cryptographer whose Hashcash system helped lay the groundwork for Bitcoin’s proof-of-work mechanism, told Cointelegraph that conventional MPC protocols are often too complex and require too much communication between devices to be practical for fully offline cold storage.

“When people talk about MPC, they’re talking about some very esoteric and complicated protocols that are hard to secure and are very interactive. So you can’t really use them in a cold storage setting,” Back said.

Related: Blockstream rejects ransom as Liquid hackers hold nearly 600 BTC

Adam Back makes the case for simpler Bitcoin custody

Back pointed to the Binance $6.3 billion hack as an example of the risks facing internet-connected custody infrastructure, arguing that keeping signing devices offline can help prevent unauthorized access.

According to Binance’s investigation, attackers compromised employee devices and obtained credentials that allowed them to access the exchange’s wallet-signing infrastructure.

If you connect equipment to the internet, even if it’s via firewalls and so on, there is risk that you can get unauthorized access. You can get hackers into the network, get hackers with access to logins they shouldn’t have and so on.

He also said that AI could make existing security challenges more difficult to manage, particularly by helping attackers discover subtle flaws in complex MPC implementations.

“The AIs can help attackers find small implementation errors and things like that, which may not be obvious,” he said.

Asked whether the broader custody industry would adopt similar offline security models, Back said he hoped so, arguing that institutions should “adapt to the environment” by moving assets into cold storage to reduce exposure to potential AI-assisted attacks.

“Complexity is the enemy of security. And going back to basics is the answer, you know, just cold-store it,” Back added.

title: Inside Prediction Markets: Kalshi Eyes $65B Valuation in the Shadow of State Bans
summary:
The prediction-market sector is manoeuvring between an escalating legal war of attrition and commercial euphoria. 
While state courts pushed their enforcement perimeter beyond retail apps and straight into clearing, platforms continued to print record volume with the CFTC playing the surreal dual ro...
content:
2026-11-13T23:14:00.000+02:00

Friday, 13/11/2026 | 21:14 GMT by Tanya Chepkova

  • State pushback escalated as a Louisiana court ordered 10 operators to halt trading, brokering, and clearing.
  • Nine platforms processed $30.4 billion in weekly notional volume, as Kalshi weighed fresh funding at $65 billion.

The prediction-market sector is manoeuvring between an escalating legal war of attrition and commercial euphoria.

While state courts pushed their enforcement perimeter beyond retail apps and straight into clearing, platforms continued to print record volume with the CFTC playing the surreal dual role of industry protector and internal prosecutor.

Louisiana Extends Restrictions to Brokers and Clearers

On November 12, a Louisiana court ordered ten prediction-market operators to block users in the state, including Kalshi, Polymarket US and Robinhood. The court order goes beyond the apps: the operators may not broker, clear or settle event contracts for anyone in Louisiana.

Meanwhile, new platforms continue entering the market via partnerships. A Canadian sports prediction-market company, Prospect Markets, launched in the US as an introducing broker on Crypto.com’s infrastructure.

A day earlier, Underdog, which runs its own CFTC-registered exchange, agreed to make its contracts available through Plaee, whose clients will be able to offer those contracts under their own brands without registering as an exchange.

Crypto.com and Underdog are both among the operators named in Louisiana’s order.

The CFTC Is Fighting a Two-Front War

The CFTC continue fighting the states in court. On November 12, the agency and the United States sued Arkansas to stop its case against Kalshi. They argue that the contracts fall under federal derivatives law.

The same agency is also scrutinising Kalshi. Politico and Reuters reported that the CFTC had privately warned Kalshi it could face charges over how it notified the agency of new contracts.

Kalshi told CNBC the issue was a procedural error involving a handful of contracts, many of which were not live.

Kalshi Eyes $65B Valuation Leap

DeFi Rate recorded about $30.4 billion in notional volume across nine venues for November 7–12, with Kalshi accounting for roughly 78% of that volume.

At the same time, the platform is discussing new funding at a $65 billion valuation, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters on November 12. That would be $25 billion more than the $40 billion post-money valuation of its Series G two weeks earlier.

Polymarket reported revenue growth and job cuts in the same week. On November 10, it told CNBC that its annualised revenue had passed $1.8 billion, up from more than $1 billion in June. That figure is the company’s own run rate, not full-year revenue.

The next day, it confirmed that it had cut jobs and ended contractor agreements. It said the reorganisation followed leadership changes and also included new hires.

The prediction-market sector is manoeuvring between an escalating legal war of attrition and commercial euphoria.

While state courts pushed their enforcement perimeter beyond retail apps and straight into clearing, platforms continued to print record volume with the CFTC playing the surreal dual role of industry protector and internal prosecutor.

Louisiana Extends Restrictions to Brokers and Clearers

On November 12, a Louisiana court ordered ten prediction-market operators to block users in the state, including Kalshi, Polymarket US and Robinhood. The court order goes beyond the apps: the operators may not broker, clear or settle event contracts for anyone in Louisiana.

Meanwhile, new platforms continue entering the market via partnerships. A Canadian sports prediction-market company, Prospect Markets, launched in the US as an introducing broker on Crypto.com’s infrastructure.

A day earlier, Underdog, which runs its own CFTC-registered exchange, agreed to make its contracts available through Plaee, whose clients will be able to offer those contracts under their own brands without registering as an exchange.

Crypto.com and Underdog are both among the operators named in Louisiana’s order.

The CFTC Is Fighting a Two-Front War

The CFTC continue fighting the states in court. On November 12, the agency and the United States sued Arkansas to stop its case against Kalshi. They argue that the contracts fall under federal derivatives law.

The same agency is also scrutinising Kalshi. Politico and Reuters reported that the CFTC had privately warned Kalshi it could face charges over how it notified the agency of new contracts.

Kalshi told CNBC the issue was a procedural error involving a handful of contracts, many of which were not live.

Kalshi Eyes $65B Valuation Leap

DeFi Rate recorded about $30.4 billion in notional volume across nine venues for November 7–12, with Kalshi accounting for roughly 78% of that volume.

At the same time, the platform is discussing new funding at a $65 billion valuation, a person familiar with the matter told Reuters on November 12. That would be $25 billion more than the $40 billion post-money valuation of its Series G two weeks earlier.

Polymarket reported revenue growth and job cuts in the same week. On November 10, it told CNBC that its annualised revenue had passed $1.8 billion, up from more than $1 billion in June. That figure is the company’s own run rate, not full-year revenue.

The next day, it confirmed that it had cut jobs and ended contractor agreements. It said the reorganisation followed leadership changes and also included new hires.

title: Kraken parent Payward gains market share as slower trading weighs on earnings
summary: Payward’s adjusted EBITDA fell 66% year over year to $60 million, even as its share of global spot trading nearly doubled and fee-based services expanded.
content:
Kraken’s parent company Payward nearly doubled its share of global crypto spot trading to 6.5% in September from 3.3% a year earlier, even as weaker trading activity weighed on its earnings.

The market-share gain means Payward captured a larger portion of spot trading relative to competitors, rather than an increase in trading activity across its platforms. The company handled $353 billion in transactions in the third quarter, down 30% from a year earlier, according to financial results released Friday.

The two figures measure different things. The market share tracks its portion of global spot trading across its platforms in September, compared with a year earlier, while Payward’s quarterly transaction volume includes activity across multiple products, including spot, margin, equities, payments and certain derivatives.

Adjusted EBITDA fell to $60 million from the $178.6 million reported a year earlier. Total platform margin fell 12% to $487 million. Payward introduced that measure this quarter to replace adjusted revenue, adding a deduction for staking rewards paid to customers.

Acquisitions expand Payward beyond spot trading

Payward has spent the past two years expanding beyond its core cryptocurrency exchange business through acquisitions in derivatives, proprietary trading, tokenized assets and payments. The strategy aims to diversify revenue beyond transaction fees, which fluctuate with market activity.

Its purchases include futures broker NinjaTrader and proprietary trading firm Breakout in 2025, followed by the acquisition of US-regulated derivatives platform Bitnomial in May 2026. The company also expanded into stablecoin payments with its purchase of Reap in July.

Those businesses contributed to a broader mix of trading and service-based activity in the third quarter. The number of derivatives contracts on which Payward charges a per-contract fee rose 84% to 66 million. Margin from subscriptions, trader evaluations and other paid services rose 59% to $125 million.

Breakout, which charges traders for evaluations that can qualify them for funded trading accounts, was included for the full quarter after joining in September 2025. The July purchase of Reap added a stablecoin payments and card-issuing business. The company did not quantify either acquisition’s contribution to the quarter.

Related: Kraken parent Payward acquires Magic Labs’ wallet business

Earnings recover from second-quarter lows

Results improved from the second quarter despite remaining below year-earlier levels. Total transaction volume rose 22%, while total platform margin increased 12% to $487 million from $436 million.

The improvement was not driven by trading alone. Margin earned from assets customers hold on Payward’s platforms, including staking-related services, rose 26% to $128 million. That accounted for roughly half of the $51 million quarterly increase in total platform margin.

Adjusted EBITDA climbed to $60 million from $23 million, while its margin relative to total platform margin rose to 12% from 5%. Compared with a year earlier, however, adjusted EBITDA was down 66%, underscoring the pressure on profitability despite a growing contribution from services less directly tied to trading activity. Asset- and access-based services accounted for 52% of total platform margin, up from 46% a year earlier.

That shift could matter for an eventual public listing. Payward confidentially filed for a US IPO in November 2025 but paused its plans in March as market conditions weakened. By September, the earliest potential listing window under consideration was the second quarter of 2027.

title: US regulators move ahead on crypto trust charters as Senate scrutiny grows
summary: Coinbase’s trust company received final clearance as lawmakers seek records on crypto firms’ compliance and potential conflicts of interest.
content:
Latest NewsPublishedNov 13, 2026

Coinbase’s trust company received final clearance as lawmakers seek records on crypto firms’ compliance and potential conflicts of interest.

Federal regulators are opening more avenues for crypto companies to operate under US rules, while congressional investigators are asking to see the records behind those decisions. Lawmakers want to know how regulators justified new trust charters, how crypto companies handled compliance and what dealings they had with people tied to President Donald Trump’s administration.

On Nov. 9, Coinbase announced that its national trust company had received final approval to open. The Office of the Comptroller of the Currency granted preliminary conditional approval in April. The company said the charter gives its custody business a consistent federal framework.

Lawmakers had been questioning how federal regulators were using their existing authority to expand crypto companies’ reach. In a May 18 letter to the OCC, Sen. Elizabeth Warren challenged at least nine crypto trust-charter approvals, including Coinbase’s earlier conditional approval. She asked for the applications, the legal analyses behind the approvals and any related communications between OCC officials and the White House or Trump family.

Four days before Coinbase’s announcement, Sen. Richard Blumenthal renewed demands for records from Binance, Tether and two Trump-linked ventures. He gave them until Jan. 4, 2027, to turn over the requested records voluntarily and warned that his subcommittee could take other steps to obtain them.

title: DeepSeek’s AI Models Carry Nvidia Blackwell ‘Fingerprints,’ Researcher Says
summary: Will DePue’s analysis claims hidden numerical patterns reveal Blackwell access at DeepSeek and three other Chinese labs, reopening questions about AI chip controls.
content:
Skip to content
Assets: NVDA

Will DePue’s analysis claims hidden numerical patterns reveal Blackwell access at DeepSeek and three other Chinese labs, reopening questions about AI chip controls.

Researcher Will DePue says the numbers inside DeepSeek’s AI models carry a hidden Nvidia Blackwell fingerprint, raising fresh questions about Chinese developers’ access to restricted American computing hardware.

His claim spans six models from DeepSeek, Moonshot AI, MiniMax and Ant Group. The unusual evidence trail is the models’ publicly released weights: the enormous collections of numbers that determine how they work.

But the distinction between a striking technical finding and a proven export-control breach matters. The research identifies patterns left when models were initialised. It cannot, by itself, establish where the hardware was located or how access was obtained.

DeepSeek Blackwell claim turns model weights into evidence

“This evidence isn’t based on any insider information or leaking,” DePue wrote in his post on X. He says he searched more than six trillion combinations of hardware layout and random seed to find matches in published models.

The premise is that initialisation leaves a numerical trace. Before training adjusts a model’s weights, software must generate their starting values. DePue argues that how a GPU distributes that work can leave a recognisable pattern that survives subsequent training.

In plain language, the claim is that the finished model still contains clues about the machinery that first set it up. That would make releasing weights a form of transparency extending beyond the model’s capabilities to aspects of its production history.

What the hardware tests showed

DePue says a Blackwell B300 reproduced 445 entire preserved rows in DeepSeek-V4-Flash bit for bit, while a Hopper H100 did not. He also reports reproducing Kimi K3’s pattern on a rented GB200. These are his reported tests; BNC has not independently reproduced them.

DePue has also published a verification repository with selected weight rows and scripts for five models, including the older DeepSeek-V3. It lets readers replay these comparisons; releasing code is not the same as an independent replication.

The November 12 Unemployment Labs report associates DeepSeek-V4-Flash and MiniMax-M3 with B200/B300-compatible patterns. DeepSeek-V4-Pro, Kimi K3, Kimi K3.1-Pro and Ant Group’s Ling-3.1-flash match GB200/GB300-compatible layouts. The method does not distinguish individual chip models within those groups.

There is an established reason to care about the exact environment in these comparisons. PyTorch’s reproducibility documentation explains that fixed seeds can reproduce random sequences under controlled conditions, while identical seeds do not guarantee identical results across platforms, versions or CPU and GPU execution.

That documentation does not verify DePue’s findings. It helps explain why a convincing reproduction must specify the software, hardware and settings, rather than rely on a matching seed alone. The engineering details are part of the evidence, not incidental background.

The limits are as important as the fingerprint

An unusually configured AMD MI300X can mimic these layouts. The report excludes that alternative for V4-Flash, but not the other five models. Initialisation also need not use the hardware that subsequently trains a model.

The report is explicit that its findings “do not establish where the chips were located, how access was obtained, or whether export controls were violated.” A hardware match therefore cannot be read as a customs record or proof of a shipment into China.

Those qualifications leave room for a consequential result without accepting every broader inference attached to it. Evidence about one stage of model development can be valuable even when the rest of the supply chain remains unknown.

Why the export-control question is live

The political context predates this report. In February, Reuters quoted a senior Trump administration official alleging that DeepSeek had trained a model on Blackwell despite U.S. restrictions. The official did not disclose how the government obtained its information. That earlier allegation is context, not independent confirmation of DePue’s new tests.

The legal framework also reaches beyond a simple map of chip locations. In May 31 guidance, the Bureau of Industry and Security said pre-existing licensing requirements continued to apply to covered advanced-computing items destined for certain China- or Macau-headquartered entities, including entities outside those destinations, unless an applicable exception was available.

That guidance concerns specified transactions and regulated items. Establishing a violation would require evidence about the parties, permissions and circumstances involved. A technical paper can raise questions for investigators without answering every legal element itself.

Running DeepSeek on Blackwell is a different question

Nvidia’s own technical documentation already describes serving DeepSeek-V4 on Blackwell and Hopper systems. That is inference: running a released model to produce answers. DePue’s analysis concerns the hardware used to generate starting weights, with possible implications for training.

Confusing those stages would make ordinary deployment documentation look like evidence of the disputed development process. It is not. An open model can run on hardware different from the equipment that originally created it.

For investors, the broader issue is how hardware access shapes AI competition and the economics of supplying computing capacity. BNC’s CoreWeave earnings analysis examined the financing burden behind that infrastructure buildout. This report adds a different question: how much outsiders can learn about computing access from the models themselves.

The next useful evidence would be independent reproductions, scrutiny of alternative explanations and responses addressing the findings from the companies named. For now, DePue has supplied a detailed, testable claim. The intrigue lies in what the numbers might reveal—and in the gap between identifying a machine’s trace and reconstructing how it came to be used.

title: OneRoyal Veteran Gebran Massabni Joins PrimaCapital as General Manager
summary:
PrimaCapital has named Gebran Massabni as its new General Manager. He is another former OneRoyal executive joining the management team at the retail FX and CFD broker founded by Ali Marwani. 
Massabni comes to PrimaCapital after spending over 17 years at OneRoyal, where he held several senior roles,...
content:
2026-11-13T21:33:10.816+02:00

Friday, 13/11/2026 | 19:33 GMT by Tanya Chepkova

  • Gebran Massabni joins PrimaCapital after more than 17 years at OneRoyal.
  • He reunites with several OneRoyal alumni at PrimaCapital, including founder Ali Marwani.

PrimaCapital has named Gebran Massabni as its new General Manager. He is another former OneRoyal executive joining the management team at the retail FX and CFD broker founded by Ali Marwani.

Massabni comes to PrimaCapital after spending over 17 years at OneRoyal, where he held several senior roles, including Head of Business Development and Chief Operating Officer. In 2023 he was named Head of Global Sales.

Massabni’s new role at PrimaCapital appears in the speaker program for the Forex Traders Expo & Summit Dubai, which takes place later this month. However, PrimaCapital has not shared details about his responsibilities or when he will officially start.

PrimaCapital Builds Team around OneRoyal

Alumni Massabni is joining a company that already has ties to his previous employer. Marwani started PrimaCapital in 2023 after spending ten years at OneRoyal and its predecessor, Royal Financials, which he joined in 2011. Both companies work in the retail trading sector and offer leveraged products like FX and CFDs.

Massabni brings experience from a well-established, multi-licensed broker to a newer company that competes in similar markets, especially in the Middle East.

He is not the only former OneRoyal employee at PrimaCapital. Public records show that Mohammad Jawad Rashid is now Head of Risk at PrimaCapital after previously working as Head of Market Research at OneRoyal.

It is unclear if these hires are part of a planned recruitment strategy.

UAE Activities Run through a Separate Company

According to its website, PrimaCapital’s main operating company is PrimaCapital Limited, which is registered in Saint Lucia under number 2023-00550. The broker provides CFDs through MetaTrader 5.

PrimaCapital’s activities in the UAE are more limited in scope. The company says that all introducing activities in the country are handled only by Prima Global Financials LLC, which holds a Category 5 licence from the UAE Capital Market Authority.

This licence allows for client introductions and promotion, but not full brokerage or execution services in the UAE. This is an important distinction as Massabni steps into his new role as General Manager.

Why Private AI is More Important Than Ever

content:
Mark Suman, co-founder and CEO of Maple AI, joins BMTV to talk about private AI built so that even its own team cannot read your chats. He says AI is weaving its way into every aspect of life, including financial transactions and agents paying each other, and he would not want those chats read by a company whose source code you cannot inspect. Maple was built from the ground up with open-source code and encryption. Much like Bitcoin, he wants people not to trust the company, but to verify. All of your data, all of your thoughts, everything that’s precious to you stays encrypted all the way throughout the pipeline, and he says you do not have to sacrifice security to use the best open-weight models.

title: Coincheck Scraps Aplo Brokerage in $18.8M Reversal, Folding Tech into 3iQ
summary:
Coincheck Group is winding down its French institutional crypto prime broker, Aplo, just 13 months after acquisition. 
The group recorded an $18.8 million impairment tied to Aplo for the quarter ended September, contributing to a $26.3 million net quarterly loss, compared with a $2.3 million profit ...
content:
2026-11-13T19:58:47.139+02:00

Friday, 13/11/2026 | 17:58 GMT by Tanya Chepkova

  • Aplo has closed onboarding and entered a phased withdrawal mode through 27 January.
  • Coincheck is repurposing Aplo architecture to power segregated institutional crypto portfolios (SMAs) under its 3iQ subsidiary.

Coincheck Group is winding down its French institutional crypto prime broker, Aplo, just 13 months after acquisition.

The group recorded an $18.8 million impairment tied to Aplo for the quarter ended September, contributing to a $26.3 million net quarterly loss, compared with a $2.3 million profit a year earlier.

The Tokyo-listed crypto fintech giant abandoned the idea to run a standalone European brokerage. Aplo will end its client services by 12 February 2027, and its intellectual property and trading architecture will become a part of a newly created asset-management subsidiary, 3iQ.

A Three-Month Runway to Unwind Balances

Aplo announced the decision to cease operations on 12 November, immediately closing its doors to new accounts and notifying the institutional clients of the termination of their service agreement.

Under the contractual notice period, Aplo has three months to wind down operations and withdraw funds. All accounts will be switched to “withdraw-only” mode no later than 27 January 2027.

Clients can convert holdings into USDC, EURC, or fiat before sweeping funds to external wallets or bank accounts. Any assets remaining by the February cut-off will be liquidated into euros and wired to clients’ registered bank accounts.

Aplo reported no balance-sheet holes or frozen assets, noting that French regulators are notified of the process. Furthermore, Coincheck highlighted Aplo’s MiCA-compliant status, indicating the closure was driven by commercial viability rather than regulatory rejection.

Technology Harvested for 3iQ’s Managed Accounts

Coincheck acquired Aplo in October 2025, when the brokerage served more than 60 active institutional clients, with plans to expand Aplo’s liquidity access, financing products and execution services for banks and institutional investors.

Thirteen months later, management decided that its technology has greater value inside 3iQ than in a small standalone European brokerage.

Approximately half of Aplo’s current employees have been invited to join 3iQ and work on the separately managed account product.

The project will use Aplo’s software and infrastructure to launch managed crypto accounts (SMAs) for institutions and high-net-worth investors in the first half of 2027.

The ultimate test of the retreat now shifts to execution: whether salvaging Aplo’s code for 3iQ can justify the write-down and recoup value from an acquisition that unravelled in barely a year.
